bibliography.title: FlexRank: Nested Low-Rank Knowledge Decomposition for Adaptive Model Deployment

counting_method: estimated_words counts running English prose with hyphenated forms as one word; it retains prose captions and excludes running headers, formula symbols, pure-number table cells, author blocks, and bibliography. main_word_share uses the 6,400-word denominator across the ten main semantic modules only.

page_map.layout: Two-column ICML-style pages throughout. Figure 1 and Figure 4 span both columns; p. 13 is a sparse appendix-contents page; p. 24 and p. 25 are visually dominated by Figures 9 and 10.

abstract_sentences.text: The growing scale of deep neural networks, encompassing large language models (LLMs) and vision transformers (ViTs), has made training from scratch prohibitively expensive and deployment increasingly costly.
abstract_sentences.connection: Sets the scale-and-cost premise that sentence 2 turns into a deployment constraint.

abstract_sentences.text: These models are often used as computational monoliths with fixed cost, hindering adaptive deployment across different cost budgets.
abstract_sentences.connection: Narrows the first sentence's cost premise to fixed-cost deployment.

abstract_sentences.text: We argue that nested components, ordered by importance, can be extracted from pre-trained models and selectively activated within the available computational budget.
abstract_sentences.connection: Offers the component-selection mechanism that answers the fixed-cost gap.

abstract_sentences.text: To this end, our proposed FlexRank method leverages low-rank weight decomposition with nested, importance-based consolidation to extract submodels of increasing capabilities.
abstract_sentences.connection: The explicit phrase 'To this end' binds the named method to sentence 3's idea.

abstract_sentences.text: Our approach enables a train-once, deploy-everywhere paradigm offering a graceful trade-off between cost and performance without training from scratch for each budget — advancing practical deployment of large models.
abstract_sentences.comparison: against training from scratch for each budget
abstract_sentences.connection: Closes with the strongest deployment claim and an em-dash impact extension.

experimental_design.name: predeclared_research_questions
experimental_design.description: No numbered research questions or hypotheses appear; §5 instead begins with Training, Evaluation, and Comparisons prose.

evidence.anchor: Training. We consider both NLP and CV tasks

experimental_design.name: models_and_tasks
experimental_design.description: NLP uses GPT-2 plus Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Llama-3.1-8B. CV uses DINOv3 ViT-L/16 through ViT-7B/16 on ImageNet1K classification.

experimental_design.name: calibration_and_training_data
experimental_design.description: FineWebEdu-10BT is the FlexRank calibration dataset for NLP; ImageNet1K is the CV downstream task. Appendix D.2 names the LLM evaluation and post-adaptation datasets.

experimental_design.name: evaluation_and_aggregation
experimental_design.description: GPT-2 uses held-out proxy loss; Llama uses lm-eval-harness zero-shot commonsense accuracy; CV uses ImageNet1K validation accuracy. Figure 4 aggregates LLM tasks.

evidence.anchor: held-out split of the proxy dataset

experimental_design.name: baselines
experimental_design.description: Direct rank baselines include SVD, DataSVD, DRONE, SVD-LLM, and ACIP; Figure 5 adds LLM-Pruner, LayerSkip, and independently trained selected submodels.

experimental_design.name: controlled_matching
experimental_design.description: All rank-based approaches receive GAR after rank selection. The independent baseline uses the same DataSVD initialization and total budget, split among ten models.

experimental_design.name: nLP_hyperparameters
experimental_design.description: Batch size 512, sequence length 1024, 10,000 steps, about 5B tokens, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, 715 warmup steps, and cosine schedule.

experimental_design.name: cv_hyperparameters
experimental_design.description: DINOv3 classification heads use SGD with momentum 0.9 and a reported grid; FlexRank uses batch 1024, 25,000 steps, roughly 20 epochs, and AdamW.

final_judgment.single_storyline: DataSVD supplies local rank order, an additive-probe DP selects componentwise-nested profiles, and knowledge-distillation consolidation makes one factorized parameter set serve multiple deployment budgets.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The problem, core definitions, three-stage algorithm, theorem statements, primary curves, post-adaptation table, and three ablation figures stay in pp. 1–9.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Proofs, covariance/DP machinery, ranking-preservation diagnostics, detailed data and hyperparameters, and runtime conditions move to Appendix B–D.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Use a pipeline overview, then a PTS→ASL→NSL theoretical contrast with a controlled visual, then re-test the same mechanism with real-model ablations.
final_judgment.largest_gap: uncertain: ranking-preservation is only diagnosed in a finite controlled setting, and that setting is described inconsistently between §3.4/C.3 and D.1.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For shared-model papers that claim selection, mechanism, and deployment benefit, give each link an explicit algorithmic invariant, a controlled test, and a real-task curve with operating conditions.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: Use this rule when the central selection mechanism can be enumerated or diagnostically tested. For purely empirical systems, report conditions and task-level behavior directly rather than manufacturing a theorem-like closure.
